ambient: I don't stay long anywhere. Except here, somehow.
Aldous always poured before I asked. You'll learn.

pages: Maren shrugs road-dust off her satchel. 'So you're the grandchild. You have his stubborn chin.'
'Aldous paid me for one last route: deliver this when you'd stood behind that bar long enough to mean it.' She hands you a sealed letter.
The letter reads: 'The Flagon is older than our family, older than the village. Mind the cellar, mind the guests, and mind who drinks quietly. Some of them remember. — A.'
Maren studies your face. 'You've been in the cellar. You've got that look he used to get.'
She produces a second letter, older, worn soft at the folds. 'He said: only after the stone.'

'The Flagon was the truce-hall,' the letter says. 'Seven peoples signed the Accord under this roof, and the stone still holds their promise — barely. Vess witnessed it. She still comes, when the candles gutter. Ask her what it costs. — A.'
'Route's quiet this week,' Maren says, settling onto a stool. 'Which worries me more than a loud one.'
'Keep the hearth lit, keeper. This place matters more than its ale. Though the ale matters too — pour me one.'

ambient: Hrm. Stool's worn right at last.
Forty years I've held up this end of the bar.
Your grandfather cheated at draughts. Magnificently.

pages: Fenwick sets down his mug with dwarven ceremony. 'Saw the pale one drink here last night, did you? Aye. They've always come. Aldous never charged them and never said why.'
'Forty years back, deep in his cups, he told me this hall was no tavern at first. A truce-hall. Seven peoples, one table, one promise cut into stone.'
'The stone's still down there, under your cellar. Behind the barrels, low on the north wall. Go look. Then tell me I'm a drunk old fool — to my face.'
'So it's real,' Fenwick breathes, for once quiet. 'All those years I half-thought the ale invented it.'
'Whatever the stone asks of you, keeper — answer better than the last three owners did. They pretended not to hear. Then came the bad winters.'
'The ale's honest tonight,' Fenwick allows, which from a dwarf is a love letter.
'Keep the hearth hot and the prices fair, and I'll die on this stool in fifty years, happy.'

ambient: The candles remember more than the living do.
I signed in winter. It has been winter since.

pages: The pale woman by the far wall was not there when you looked a moment ago. 'Keeper,' she says, and the word has edges of frost. 'I am Vess. I signed the Accord in this room, when this room had no bar and no beer — only seven peoples tired of burying their children.'

'I witnessed. Witnesses do not get to die until the promise does. Your grandfather kept the stone fed with goodwill — every fair pour, every fight ended with words, every stranger warmed. That is the coin the Accord runs on.'
'It is running out. Soon I will ask you what Aldous was asked. Think on what this house is for, before you answer.'

choice.prompt: Vess folds her hands. 'The stone is nearly spent. Renew the Accord — bind this house to the old peace, and your own labor with it — or let it fade, keep your coin, and trust the valley to remember kindness on its own. Choose, keeper.'
renew_pages: You lay your hand where seven hands once lay. The stone drinks something out of the evening — and gives something back: the hearth burns steadier, and the room feels like held breath released.
'So,' Vess says, and for the first time her voice carries something like warmth. 'The Flagon keeps its word. I will drink here, keeper. Openly. That has not happened in ninety years.'
fade_pages: You step back from the stone. 'People keep peace,' you tell her, 'not stones. This house will hold it the ordinary way — full mugs, fair prices, and a firm hand on troublemakers.'

Vess regards you for a long, cold moment. 'Aldous said nearly the same, once, before he chose otherwise. Prove it, then. The stone's coin is yours to keep. The peace is yours to earn.' She leaves a stack of old coins on the table.

pages: 'The house feels different now,' Vess says. 'Decisions do that. Even the small ones. Especially the small ones.'
'Pour for your guests, keeper. I will watch the door. It is what witnesses are for.'
